justice: Both sides of the street appear to have pedestrian space, but the right side allocates a large frontage area to parked scooters, reducing balanced access to curbside space for all users.
The carriageway is wide and unobstructed for motor vehicles, while there is no clearly marked dedicated bicycle facility, indicating a stronger spatial preference for driving than for cycling.
Sidewalk surfaces appear mostly flat and continuous in sections, but there are no visible tactile paving strips, marked curb ramps, or other explicit universal-access features in the image.
safety: Motor traffic appears light and the street is relatively wide, which lowers immediate conflict frequency, but the broad open roadway may also encourage higher vehicle speeds.
There is no visible marked crosswalk, refuge island, or other pedestrian crossing treatment in the visible segment, weakening crossing safety for people on foot.
Scooters are parked densely along the right-side pedestrian zone, which can create edge friction and reduce clear walking space near the curb.
Streetlights are present along the corridor, which supports basic nighttime visibility, but overhead utility lines and a visually open roadside edge suggest limited protection from roadside hazards.
livability: Ground-floor shops on the left side provide everyday commercial activity and support local daily needs within walking distance.
A visible public-service sign on the left building suggests some community-serving function, which adds practical neighborhood value beyond retail.
The street has some trees and a relatively calm traffic environment, making it more usable for routine local movement than a heavily arterial road.
However, the right side includes a blank wall/open edge and large paved frontage areas, which reduce street enclosure and active frontage compared with more vibrant main streets.
sustainability: Street trees on both sides contribute modest shade and urban greening, improving ecological performance compared with a fully paved corridor.
The presence of many scooters indicates support for smaller, lower-energy local travel modes, even though their parking is not well organized.
No dedicated bike lane, visible bus stop, or public transit infrastructure is evident, limiting stronger support for sustainable mode shift.
Large expanses of asphalt roadway and hard paving dominate the scene, and there are no visible rain gardens, permeable strips, or stormwater features.
aesthetics: The row of low-rise shopfronts creates a coherent neighborhood street wall and gives the street a recognizable local character.
Street trees add rhythm and soften the corridor, improving visual quality compared with a fully exposed commercial strip.
Colorful overhead flags introduce visual interest and make the street feel more festive and place-specific.
At the same time, parked scooters, exposed utility wires, and a blank wall on the right reduce overall visual neatness and refinement.
comfort: Trees provide intermittent shade, but canopy coverage is incomplete and much of the street and sidewalk remains exposed to strong sun, limiting thermal comfort.
Sidewalk and frontage surfaces appear mostly smooth and level, supporting basic physical comfort for walking and rolling.
There are no visible benches, shelters, or resting facilities, reducing comfort for people who need to pause or wait.
Low traffic volumes likely reduce noise stress and improve psychological comfort, but the open roadway and lack of clear pedestrian buffering can still feel exposed.
walkability: There is pedestrian space along both sides of the street, and the corridor appears generally continuous for local walking trips.
Ground-floor shops and services on the left create destinations within short distance, which supports utilitarian walking.
Walkability is weakened by the absence of visible crosswalk markings and by the wide roadway, which makes crossing less convenient and legible.
Scooter parking on the right-side frontage can intrude into pedestrian space and reduce the clarity of the walking path.
bikeability: The roadway is relatively wide and traffic appears light, which can make basic on-street cycling possible for confident riders.
However, there is no visible protected bike lane, painted cycle lane, or dedicated cycling markings, so cyclists must mix with motor traffic.
Dense scooter parking along the right frontage suggests demand for two-wheel travel, but also indicates limited organized cycling or micromobility management.
No visible bicycle parking racks, intersection treatments, or cyclist-priority features are present to improve convenience and safety.
